clinicalPearls: Cholera is an acute toxin-mediated diarrhoeal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 or O139 (the serogroups with epidemic potential) that can progress to profound, rapidly progressive dehydration and death within hours (p.1325-1326).

After a 24-48 h incubation in a non-immune individual, illness begins with the sudden onset of painless watery diarrhoea that can rapidly become voluminous; vomiting is common and fever is usually absent (p.1327).

The characteristic stool is non-bilious, gray, slightly cloudy fluid flecked with mucus, containing no blood, with a fishy, inoffensive odour, described as rice-water stool because it resembles water in which rice has been washed (p.1327).
In severe cases (cholera gravis) volume loss can exceed 250 mL/kg in the first 24 h, and muscle cramps from electrolyte disturbance are common (p.1327).

Symptoms parallel the degree of volume contraction: thirst at <5% body-weight loss; postural hypotension, weakness, tachycardia and decreased skin turgor at 5-10%; and oliguria, weak or absent pulses, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), wrinkled washerwoman skin, somnolence and coma at >10% (p.1327-1328).
If fluids and electrolytes are replaced adequately, complications are averted and the illness is self-limited, resolving in a few days (p.1328).
harrison.pathophysiology: Cholera is fundamentally a toxin-mediated disease. After ingestion (most often via faecally contaminated water, though contaminated food and human-to-human transmission also contribute), V. cholerae colonises the small intestine, a process dependent on the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP), with cholera toxin, TCP and other virulence factors coordinately regulated by ToxR and by quorum sensing. The organism elaborates cholera toxin, a protein enterotoxin made of a monomeric enzymatic A subunit and a pentameric B-subunit binding moiety. The B pentamer binds GM1 ganglioside on the epithelial cell surface, delivering the A subunit, whose activated form (A1) irreversibly ADP-ribosylates the GTP-binding regulatory component of adenylate cyclase. This upregulates adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cyclic AMP, which inhibits absorptive sodium transport in villus cells and activates secretory chloride transport in crypt cells, driving accumulation of sodium chloride in the lumen; water follows passively to maintain osmolality, producing isotonic fluid that exceeds the gut's reabsorptive capacity and results in watery diarrhoea. Cholera toxin also enhances secretion via prostaglandins and/or neural histamine receptors. Unless lost fluid and electrolytes are replaced, profound dehydration leads to hypovolaemic shock and bicarbonate loss leads to acidosis. The cholera toxin genes (ctxAB) are carried on the bacteriophage CTX-phi, which uses TCP as its receptor, allowing horizontal transfer to generate new toxigenic strains (p.1326-1327).
additionalDifferentials: Other secretory/toxigenic watery diarrhoeas: enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (produces a heat-labile toxin like cholera toxin), and other dehydrating secretory diarrhoeal illnesses to which the term cholera has historically and loosely been applied (p.1325)
Diarrhoea due to non-O1/O139 (noncholera) V. cholerae, which generally do not produce cholera toxin and do not cause large epidemics (p.1330)
infectionMimics: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (heat-labile enterotoxin resembling cholera toxin causing secretory diarrhoea) (p.1325-1326)
Other Vibrio gastroenteritis, e.g. Vibrio parahaemolyticus and non-O1/O139 V. cholerae (p.1330)
nonInfectiousMimics: Severely dehydrating secretory diarrhoea of non-infectious aetiology, to which the term cholera has at times been loosely applied (p.1325)
additionalInvestigations: Stool culture on a selective medium such as taurocholate-tellurite-gelatin (TTG) agar or thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose (TCBS) agar; the organism must be specifically sought (p.1328)
Direct dark-field microscopy of a wet mount of fresh stool, with serotype discernible by immobilisation with specific antisera (p.1328)
Point-of-care antigen-detection cholera dipstick (rapid diagnostic test) for field use or where laboratory facilities are lacking (p.1328)
Cary-Blair transport medium and/or alkaline-peptone water-enrichment medium if sample processing will be delayed (p.1328)
Vibrios are oxidase-positive; standard Enterobacteriaceae biochemical testing suffices for identification (p.1328)

Supportive labs in dehydrated patients: elevated haematocrit (haemoconcentration) in non-anaemic patients, mild neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised blood urea nitrogen and creatinine (prerenal azotaemia), normal sodium/potassium/chloride, markedly reduced bicarbonate (<15 mmol/L), elevated anion gap and low arterial pH (~7.2) (p.1328)
redFlags: Profound, rapidly progressive dehydration developing within hours (p.1325)
Signs of severe dehydration: unconsciousness, lethargy or floppiness, weak or absent pulse, inability to drink, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), >10% loss of body weight (p.1328)
Voluminous ongoing stool losses (volume loss exceeding 250 mL/kg in the first 24 h in severe cases) (p.1327)
Features of hypovolaemic shock, oliguria, somnolence and coma (p.1327-1328)
Acute watery diarrhoea or death from acute watery diarrhoea in a patient >=5 years, even where cholera is not known to be present (p.1328)
harrison.prognosis: Death from cholera is due to hypovolaemic shock. Historically the disease carried high mortality, but prompt aggressive fluid repletion and supportive care can obviate this. With adequate fluid and electrolyte replacement, complications are averted and the illness is self-limited, resolving over a few days. Complications derive exclusively from volume and electrolyte depletion and include renal failure due to acute tubular necrosis. Untreated cholera carries very high case-fatality (historically >50% in untreated severe cases), which falls dramatically with rehydration (p.1326, p.1328).
pitfalls: The organism is not recovered on routine media; V. cholerae must be specifically sought using selective medium, or the diagnosis will be missed (p.1328).
Diagnosis is often syndromic and many endemic countries under-report to the WHO, so the true burden and distribution are unknown and cases may be unrecognised (p.1326).
Cholera should still be suspected in severe acute watery diarrhoea or death even in areas not known to have cholera (p.1328).
Fever is usually absent, so its absence should not dissuade from the diagnosis (p.1327).
Immunity to V. cholerae O1 is not protective against O139 (and vice versa), so prior infection does not guarantee protection against the other serogroup (p.1327).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison stratifies dehydration in cholera into: (1) None or mild (diarrhoea present) - thirst in some cases, <5% loss of total body weight; (2) Moderate - thirst, postural hypotension, weakness, tachycardia, decreased skin turgor, dry mouth/tongue, no tears, 5-10% loss of total body weight; and (3) Severe - unconsciousness, lethargy or floppiness, weak or absent pulse, inability to drink, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), >10% loss of total body weight. This dehydration assessment guides the intensity of rehydration (p.1328).
